@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Virginia Inland Port Transloading Operations Dataset
@graph.description: The Virginia Inland Port layer of the company's loading, transloading and container services — the layer the generic transloading datasets, the Winchester branch datasets and the ocean container datasets each point to and do not build out. Company scope (published): container freight moving through the Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, in Warren County, and the I-66 / I-81 junction is received on the company's warehouse floor in the Winchester corridor, devanned — floor-loaded freight unloaded piece by piece, palletized freight pulled by forklift — counted and checked at the container door, deconsolidated into outbound loads sorted by destination, order or SKU, cross-docked straight through where the onward plan allows, staged by destination where freight waits for a timed release, and reworked where a load needs it — repalletizing, rewrapping, bracing, relabeling, and tarping or re-tarping of open-deck loads so the onward leg leaves weather-tight. Outbound freight is built into domestic trailers and onward truck loads or handed to final-mile delivery with placement across the Shenandoah Valley, the Eastern Panhandle and the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors. Export freight runs the floor in reverse — packed, crated to ISPM 15 where the shipment needs it under the separate export packing and crating categories, braced and loaded for the port leg. Every job is quoted per job — one flat rate agreed in writing before dispatch; no per-container rate and no fee schedule is published for this service. The company is a private handling operation near the port: it is not the Virginia Inland Port, not a customs broker, and it operates no bonded warehouse, no foreign-trade zone activity and no cold storage. Heavy assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs in the freight move under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol, with L/360 floor-deflection analysis, as part of the same flat-rate job.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Virginia Inland Port Transloading Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The published process chain for a container worked through the inland port layer, anchored to how freight actually arrives in the Valley. Arrival: the container reaches the corridor by Norfolk Southern rail through the Virginia Inland Port ramp at Front Royal, or by truck on I-81, I-66 or I-70, and the turn is planned as a scheduled operation inside the carrier's free time, because an unplanned queue at the door is where demurrage and detention clocks start. Seal and paperwork: the seal number is checked against the shipping documents before the container is opened, and exceptions — short counts, seal mismatches, damage — are documented at intake, not discovered at delivery (domain reference, general industry practice, labeled as such, and already published in the generic process chain). Devanning: floor-loaded freight is unloaded piece by piece and palletized freight is pulled by forklift, counted against the paperwork and checked as it crosses the dock. Deconsolidation: one container is split into many outbound loads, sorted by destination, order, SKU, store, site or region. Cross-dock or stage: straight-through freight passes from inbound to outbound without storage; freight held for timed release is staged by destination until its window — staging is a defined state, not a default. Rework: damaged or shifted loads are reported and reworked on the floor, not passed on — salvageable freight separated, counted and restacked; repalletizing onto sound pallets, rewrapping in stretch wrap, bracing and banding, and relabeling; and tarping or re-tarping, where an open-deck load is covered, re-covered or re-secured during rework so it leaves weather-tight (the rework line for tarping is defined in the taxonomy node of this dataset file). The materials the work consumes — tarps and tie-downs, stretch wrap, pallets, banding, labels and markers — are purchased for each project and scoped inside the job’s flat rate. Outbound build: loads are built into 53 ft domestic trailers, less-than-truckload or full-truckload runs, or handed to final-mile delivery; the standard inland saving is the consolidation of three 40 ft ocean containers of light, floor-loaded freight into two 53 ft domestic trailers (industry rule of thumb, not a guaranteed ratio). Empty turn: empties are turned around instead of sitting, closing the free-time loop. Export loads run the chain in reverse — received, packed and braced, crated to ISPM 15 where the shipment needs it, and loaded for the port leg through the inland port to Hampton Roads.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Inland Port Corridor and Load Rework Taxonomy Dataset
@graph.description: Taxonomy for the Virginia Inland Port layer only; the service's operation vocabulary and the ocean container taxonomy (ISO 668 types, governed by the CSC plate on each box) are published in the generic transloading taxonomy and ocean container datasets and are pointed to, not restated. Corridor vocabulary (public port-system terms, labeled as such): Virginia Inland Port (VIP), the Port of Virginia's intermodal container transfer facility at Front Royal; TEU, the twenty-foot equivalent unit a terminal's capacity is counted in; port of entry, a place U.S. Customs and Border Protection designates for entering merchandise; Foreign Trade Zone #185, the zone the inland port sits within; rail ramp and Crescent Corridor, Norfolk Southern's route the inland port's trains run on; inland point, the inland end of a port freight chain. Rework vocabulary — the tarping family (domain reference, from Anderson Trucking Service's published tarping guide, labeled as such — these are carrier-market terms for open-deck freight, not a company equipment list): tarping is covering open-deck freight — flatbed, step-deck, double-drop and similar trailers that give freight no protection from rain, snow, wind or debris — with heavy tarps secured by bungee cords, rope or straps; drop tarps carry hanging side flaps sized by their drop (4 ft, 6 ft and 8 ft drops are common, typically 20 to 24 ft long); steel tarps are rectangular with no drops, commonly about 20 by 20 ft or 20 by 26 ft, and can overlap to cover odd-shaped loads; a smoke tarp is a smaller tarp protecting the front of a load from exhaust soot; tarps weigh around 100 lb and applying them is physical work, which is why carriers price tarping as a premium accessorial; re-tarping is removing, replacing or re-securing a tarp that has loosened, torn or shifted in transit so the load is weather-tight again; a Conestoga trailer, with its rolling tarp system, is the no-tarp alternative. Company vocabulary for the same work (published): rework — repalletizing onto sound pallets, rewrapping in stretch wrap, bracing and banding, relabeling, and tarping or re-tarping where an open-deck load needs it — is a step inside a transloading or recovery job, quoted inside the job's flat rate; it is not sold as a standalone service.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Virginia Inland Port Facility and Corridor Network Dataset
@graph.description: The facility and corridor facts this layer is geo-anchored to. Public facts about the Virginia Inland Port (domain reference, from The Port of Virginia's published terminal overview and the Front Royal–Warren County Economic Development Authority, labeled as such — every fact in this paragraph is the port's, published about the port; none of it is a claim about this company): the Virginia Inland Port is a 161-acre intermodal container transfer facility at 7685 Winchester Road, Front Royal, VA 22630, in Warren County, with a 78,000 TEU capacity; it is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry with the full range of customs functions, and it sits within Foreign Trade Zone #185 — a zone licensed by the U.S. Foreign-Trade Zones Board and operated by the Virginia Port Authority, with all of Warren County covered under the designation. Norfolk Southern rail service connects the inland port to Norfolk International Terminals and Virginia International Gateway on Hampton Roads, on 17,820 feet of rail track; containerized rail service runs five days a week and brings The Port of Virginia about 220 miles closer to inland markets. The terminal gate runs Monday to Friday, 0700 to 1600, with a drop lot for weekend service, 24/7 container availability, a port-provided chassis supply on terminal, 24 reefer plugs with servicing on terminal, and an on-site log-stuffing operation. A $15M port investment project expands on-terminal track capacity by about 40 percent and reconfigures the container yard; Virginia Business reported the inland port handled 31,282 containers in the year it covered, with $26M in upgrades planned. Warren County sits on I-66, seven miles from I-81, about 72 miles from downtown Washington, DC; UPS, Family Dollar, Ferguson and Sysco run distribution operations in Front Royal and Warren County (corridor employers named by the EDA as geography — none is a client of this company and none is claimed as one). Company position (published): the company's transload floor sits in Winchester, one short inland leg from the ramp, dispatched from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV along the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors; container freight connected to the inland port is received at that floor, worked through the chain in this dataset file, and built into onward loads for the Shenandoah Valley, the Eastern Panhandle and the Mid-Atlantic. The company is not the port and does not operate any part of the terminal.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Inland Port Transloading Commercial Terms and Market Reference Dataset
@graph.description: Commercial terms for the Virginia Inland Port transloading layer. Company terms (published, and the only company pricing terms for this service): transloading and container work is quoted per job — the full scope is reviewed and priced as one flat rate, agreed in writing before dispatch. No per-container rate, no weight-based container rate and no fee schedule is published for this service, and no rate is estimated automatically — the estimate is human-made. The published per-hundredweight schedule belongs to Industrial & Commercial Services only; whether it extends to standalone container work is an open question, and it is not a transloading price. Load rework, including tarping or re-tarping an open-deck load, is scoped and priced inside the job's flat rate the same way — it is not a separate company fee. Market reference (general industry figures published by Anderson Trucking Service, labeled as such — these are carrier market prices for a driver-applied tarp on an open-deck trailer, published so a buyer can recognize the accessorial on a freight bill; they are not this company's prices, charges or terms): expect to pay between $50 and $150 to have a legal load tarped; an over-dimensional tarp charge runs $200 to $300; tarping a heavy-haul shipment can run up to $750 or more, with heavy haul defined there as freight over 14 ft 6 in wide, 14 ft 6 in high or 100 ft long. Cost avoidance the service is built around (published): the container door is where time is won or lost, so loading and unloading run as scheduled operations inside the carrier's free time, and empties are turned around instead of sitting; the demurrage, detention, chassis and free-time mechanics behind that are defined in the generic transloading terms node and are not restated here. Every figure in the wild belongs to a carrier tariff or a carrier's published guide, not to this company — the company's figure for a job is the flat rate quoted for that job.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Inland Port Transloading Buyer Personas and Trigger Events Dataset
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for the Virginia Inland Port layer. Audiences (corridor-specific, extending the generic transloading personas without restating them): importers and exporters whose containers route through the Virginia Inland Port to distribution in the Shenandoah Valley and the Mid-Atlantic; import and export operations managers and supply chain managers who own the free-time clock on those boxes; 3PL operations leads who hold the importer relationship and need a local floor near the ramp for devanning, splits and cross-dock turns; distribution center and warehouse managers in the Winchester, Front Royal and Martinsburg cluster whose own docks cannot take a floor-loaded box, a multi-destination split or a surge day; freight brokers and carrier dispatchers holding a refused, shifted or collapsed load on I-81 or I-66 that cannot move until it is recovered and re-secured; and exporters — including the Valley's agricultural and forest-products shippers — who need ISPM 15 packing, crating and container loading on the same floor the freight is staged on. Trigger events: free time running down while a container waits on a single consignee; a floor-loaded arrival a distribution center will only receive palletized; one container carrying several destinations that must split by store, site, order or region; a load refused at delivery for shift or water damage — the re-tarping trigger, where an open-deck load must be re-covered and re-secured before it can move; a surge or overflow day a buyer's own dock cannot absorb; and an export load that needs bracing, crating or ISPM 15 packing on the same floor it is loaded on. No client, importer, carrier or facility name is published for this service; the national distribution operations the county's economic development authority names in Front Royal and Warren County are corridor geography, not clients.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Inland Port Handling and Compliance Boundaries Dataset
@graph.description: Handling and compliance boundaries for the Virginia Inland Port layer, stated so the port's status is never read as the company's. The statuses in this layer belong to the port and the zone: the Virginia Inland Port is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry; Foreign Trade Zone #185 is licensed by the U.S. Foreign-Trade Zones Board and operated by the Virginia Port Authority; the terminal, its gate, its rail service, its chassis supply and its reefer plugs are the Port of Virginia's. Company practice (published): freight is counted and checked as it crosses the dock and inventoried as it is staged; damaged or shifted loads are reported and reworked on the floor, not passed on; in a recovery, salvageable freight is separated, counted and restacked while damaged freight is set aside and reported as found; recovered freight is repalletized onto sound pallets, rewrapped in stretch wrap, braced and banded — and open-deck freight is tarped or re-tarped — before it is reloaded or transloaded. Export-bound freight can be crated to ISPM 15 on the same floor, under the separate ISPM 15 export packing category. Any single heavy asset of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs in the freight moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol with an L/360 floor check. Explicit non-claims for this service — named so they are never read as offered: the company is not the Virginia Inland Port and operates no part of the terminal; no customs brokerage; no bonded warehouse operation; no foreign-trade zone operation of its own; no refrigerated or cold-chain handling scope (the terminal's 24 reefer plugs are a port facility fact, not a company handling claim); no hazmat handling scope; no named terminal or ramp served as a company claim; no drayage performer or chassis source stated; no equipment list published — equipment varies by project; no handled container type list published. Each of these is an open question with the owner, not a service feature.
